content:
A connection request is the only outbound action that permanently changes your own asset, and almost nobody treats it that way.

An email costs you a send. A LinkedIn connection request, if accepted, puts that person in your network for good. Your feed changes. Who sees your posts changes. The signal value of your network to everyone else changes.

Run connection requests at outbound volume for six months and you have rebuilt your professional network around a target list, which is a strange thing to do by accident.

What I'd decide before adding that step:

Whether this campaign is worth spending your network on. For a small number of high-value accounts, obviously yes. For a broad list, you are trading a durable asset for a cheap touch.

Whether the person sending is the right person. A founder's network is worth more than an SDR's, and it's usually the founder's account people want to send from precisely because of that. Spending it on volume is the fastest way to make it worth less.

Whether a message would do the job without the request. If the account can be reached another way, the request is cost with no extra benefit.

So: there's a version of a LinkedIn step that never sends a connection request at all, and for most campaigns it's the right one.

What we shipped in August, in the order it will matter to you.

LinkedIn as a real channel. LinkedIn steps run inside the same sequence as email steps, with one shared inbox and one thread per prospect. A reply on either channel stops both.

Multi-account LinkedIn. Senders became a list. You choose which accounts a campaign sends from, and each one keeps its own pacing and its own daily budget.

A reachability panel on the campaign. Before you send, you can see who on the list is actually reachable on LinkedIn and who is not, instead of finding out by spending credits.

An inbox that stops pretending. LinkedIn replies no longer render as email. There is a channel filter, and a LinkedIn step shows a dash where an open rate would be, because LinkedIn has no open tracking and a zero there would be a lie.

Account faults hold their leads. If a LinkedIn account is restricted or paused, the leads pinned to it wait rather than silently moving to a different sender and speaking to the prospect in a second voice.

Around 40 shipped changes sit behind those 5 lines.

Everyone in cold email quotes a bounce-rate limit. No mailbox provider publishes one.

The number Google actually publishes is spam complaint rate: 0.3% is the line, 0.1% is the target.

So watch the one they publish.

When someone replies with three words, sending them four paragraphs ends the conversation.

I answer short replies short. One useful thing, one question they can answer in a sentence. The heavier the ask, the easier it is to stop replying.

Most outbound budgets count the tools and stop there.

The honest cost of a meeting includes the domains, the mailboxes, the data, the person writing the sequences, and the person answering replies at 9pm because speed matters. Tools are usually under 20% of it.

Spamtraps burn domains faster than volume does, and most people running outbound have never had them explained.

Two kinds, and they mean completely different things about your list.

Pristine traps were never real addresses. Somebody seeded them on a web page specifically so scrapers would pick them up. Mail arriving at one proves the address was harvested, because there is no other way to have got it. Blocklist operators treat a pristine hit as close to conclusive.

Recycled traps are the harsher lesson. They were real mailboxes belonging to real people. The person left, the address was abandoned, it bounced for a long stretch, and then the provider reactivated it as a trap. Mail arriving at one proves you kept sending to an address that had been telling you it was dead for months.

That second category is the one that matters for most teams, because it makes bounce hygiene and trap risk the same problem. Every hard bounce left unsuppressed is a candidate for becoming a trap hit later.

Three things follow:

Suppress hard bounces permanently and immediately, across every tool that touches the list. A suppression that exists in only one platform has not happened.

Treat any list you cannot trace to its origin as suspect. Bought lists are where pristine traps live.

Stop mailing addresses that have gone quiet for a long stretch, even where nothing ever bounced. Recycled traps come from exactly that population.

You cannot check a list for traps. Nobody will tell you where they are, and that is the point of them.

Buying signals get treated as one thing.

They decay at completely different speeds, and mixing them is why signal-based lists stop working after a month. How I sort them now:

Days. A funding announcement, a leadership change, an acquisition. The window is measured in weeks and it is crowded, because every vendor with the same data source is emailing on the same day. Being fast matters less than having something to say that the other twelve emails don't.

Weeks to months. Job postings for roles that imply your problem. These stay useful until the role is filled, and nobody tells you it was filled. I re-check open roles before a follow-up goes out, because referencing a role they filled two months ago costs you more than saying nothing would have.

Months. Technology adoption, a new office, a product launch. Slower to decay, and correspondingly weaker as a reason to email today.

Structural. Company size, industry, business model. These are filters, telling you who could plausibly buy, which is a different question from who might buy now.

The mistake I made for a long time was building one list from all four and treating the whole thing as time-sensitive. Half of it wasn't, and the half that was had gone cold by the time I got to it.

Sort by decay speed, mail the fast ones first, and re-check anything you follow up on.

We found a billing bug on ourselves and it went the wrong way for the customer, so here it is.

Adding a seat mid-cycle was creating a new charge instead of updating the quantity on the existing subscription. The effect was a double-bill on the overlap: you paid for the seat twice for the remainder of that period.

It is fixed. Seat changes are prorated quantity updates now, which is what they should always have been, and the correction is applied rather than waiting for anyone to notice and ask.

Two things we are keeping from it.

Billing bugs are not like other bugs. A rendering bug annoys someone; a billing bug takes their money and makes them prove it. They earn a different level of test coverage and we have added it.

And the second: nobody reported this. It surfaced from our own reconciliation. That is the only reason it was short-lived, and it is the argument for reconciling revenue against what you think you charged, on a schedule, rather than trusting the invoice.

Whose name is on the domains decides how a bad client breakup goes.

Bought under your account, they're your asset and the client assumes otherwise. Bought under theirs, you warmed something you'll hand back.

Pick one at signing. The argument later costs far more.

SPF usually breaks in an outbound stack for a reason nobody mentions: a lookup limit.

SPF allows a maximum of 10 DNS lookups when a receiver evaluates your record. Every "include:" costs one, and several of them chain into further lookups you cannot see from your own DNS.

Add Google Workspace, then a sequencer, then a warmup provider, then whatever sends your invoices, and a stack that looks tidy quietly crosses 10. Past that the result is a permanent error, which means no aligned pass for DMARC, which means the thing you configured carefully stops doing anything.

The check takes a minute with any SPF validator that counts lookups. Run it on every sending domain, and again whenever you add a tool.

While you are there, the requirements that apply to every sender regardless of volume are worth knowing, because most coverage only discusses the bulk thresholds:

Authentication with SPF or DKIM, at minimum.
Valid forward and reverse DNS on the sending host.
TLS on transmission.
A message that conforms to the standard format.
Spam complaint rate kept low. Google publishes 0.3% as the line and treats 0.1% as the target.

The part worth updating your mental model for: enforcement changed. Non-compliant mail used to be filtered into spam. Gmail now rejects at the SMTP level, and Microsoft has been returning outright rejections on non-compliant high-volume mail since last year.

So if a setup that worked two years ago now produces unexplained rejections, check the lookup count first.

A company hiring for the role you sell to can mean they have your problem.

It can also mean they just bought a solution and are staffing it.

Same signal, opposite conclusion.

Cold email and one-click unsubscribe is a genuine debate, and the case for it is stronger than most operators think.

The alternative to an unsubscribe click is a spam complaint. One costs a contact. The other costs reputation.

The AI SDR pitch has one risk nobody prices.

Every failure mode it has is a deliverability failure, and it lands on the customer's domain rather than the vendor's.

So ask where the bill goes when it's wrong.

The multichannel bug that embarrasses you in front of a prospect: they reply on LinkedIn, and your email sequence keeps going.

It happens because most stacks track a sequence per channel. Email steps live in the email tool, LinkedIn steps somewhere else, and neither knows what the other did.

From the prospect's side there is one conversation with your company. They answered it. Then two days later a scheduled follow-up asks whether they saw the last email.

The rule that fixes it: one thread per person, and a reply on any channel stops every channel.

Three things that need to be true for that to actually work:

Replies have to be detected on both sides, which means the LinkedIn inbox is polled rather than checked by a human when they remember.

Stopping has to be immediate rather than at the next scheduled run, because the follow-up that embarrasses you is usually queued already.

And a positive reply has to notify someone. A sequence that stops correctly and then leaves an interested person waiting three days has traded one failure for a more expensive one.

Worth testing on yourself before a campaign goes out. Reply to your own sequence on the channel you'd least expect, and watch whether everything actually stops.

Database size is the easiest thing to advertise and a weak predictor of whether your campaign works.

The number that predicts it is coverage inside your specific segment. A 300M database with 4% of your niche loses to a smaller one that has most of it.

Outbound gets described as a growth channel. It behaves more like a fixed-cost distribution asset.

Domains, mailboxes and reputation take weeks to build, degrade if idle, and can't be bought back quickly at any price.

Mothballing a factory is the closer analogy.

Client offboarding is the part of agency outbound nobody documents, and it is where the lawsuits live.

The runbook I use runs in this order.

Suppression list first, before anything is disconnected. Everyone who unsubscribed, bounced or asked to be left alone. If that list only lives inside a tool you're about to disconnect, it stops existing, and the next agency mails those people. That is a compliance problem with your fingerprints on it.

Then reply threads. Live conversations belong to the client. Export them while you still have access, because the day the seat is revoked is the day someone remembers there was a deal in flight.

Then mailboxes and domains. This is decided in the contract or it is decided in an argument. Sending domains that carry the client's brand should transfer. Throwaway sending domains you bought are yours, and should be retired rather than resold, because their reputation is a story only you know.

Then the data. What you pulled for them, in a format they can open without your tooling.

Then access. Revoke access last. Every item above depends on still having it.

One thing worth putting in the contract before you ever need it: who owns the domains, and what happens to the warmed mailboxes on them. It takes one sentence at signing and a month of arguing afterwards.

The general shape here is that offboarding well is the cheapest referral source an agency has.

Everyone optimises for replies. The drop happens after, and it's bigger than anything a subject line will fix.

Between an interested reply and a held meeting there are four places to lose someone, and I've lost people at all four.

Response time. Interest has a half-life. A reply answered the same day is a conversation; the same reply answered on Thursday is a cold start with extra context.

The ask itself. "Do you have 30 minutes this week?" asks for a decision about a calendar. Offering two specific times asks for something much smaller, and the difference in conversion is large enough to be worth the extra sentence.

Booking friction. Every extra step loses people. A link showing real availability in their timezone beats a back-and-forth that takes four messages to find a slot.

The gap between booking and the meeting. This is the one people ignore. Someone who books eight days out has had a week to remember they're busy. A short confirmation with something useful in it, sent a day before, is the cheapest intervention available.

None of this is clever. It's the part that happens after the part everyone writes about.

Answering faster was the cheapest of the four.

Four checks before a campaign goes live:

Authentication passes on each sending domain.
The suppression list is loaded and current.
Reply detection is wired to a human.
The first 50 sends go out, then you stop and read what came back.

So: launch in stages.

"Sounds interesting, send me some info" is the most misread reply in outbound.

Teams count it as a win. It is usually a polite exit, and the giveaway is that it asks for something requiring no commitment from either side.

What is actually happening: the person has enough interest to be nice and not enough to spend twenty minutes. Sending a deck confirms the arrangement, because now the ball is with them, and it stays there.

What works better is answering the smaller question they didn't ask.

Reply with one specific thing relevant to their situation, and one question that needs a short answer. Not a meeting request. A question they can respond to in a sentence, which tells you whether the interest is real.

Answer it and you have a live conversation, and the meeting ask lands differently. Ignore it and you've learned that in a day rather than assuming a deck is being read for three weeks.

So: match the weight of what you send to the weight of what you got.

A small thing that changes how a LinkedIn campaign feels: knowing who is reachable before you spend anything.

On LinkedIn, a list has tiers hiding inside it. Some people can be messaged for free. Some cost a credit. Some have messaging switched off entirely and were never reachable at any price.

Most tools let you find that out by sending. You load a list, the campaign runs, and the failures teach you the composition of your own audience after the fact.

Campaigns now carry a coverage panel that answers it beforehand: how many of these people are reachable, how many are unreachable, and how many the system left unresolved.

Credits are the smaller half of why it matters. An unreachable prospect on a LinkedIn-only sequence gets no touch at all, and with nothing telling you, that looks exactly like a campaign with a bad reply rate.

Same principle as verifying an email list.

Find out what you are holding first.

Verifiers publish their false-positive rate. Almost none publish the other one.

Every address pushed into "unknown" or "catch-all" is a possible real buyer who drops out of the campaign silently.

That bucket is usually the larger of the two, and nobody is measured on it.

Addresses that never bounce and never reply feel harmless. They're the riskiest part of an old list.

That population is where abandoned mailboxes sit, and abandoned mailboxes are what providers turn into traps.

So retire silent contacts on a schedule.

A pipeline number built from meetings booked is a forecast of your calendar.

A pipeline number built from meetings held, each with a named next step, is a forecast of your quarter. Most outbound reporting quietly does the first and calls it the second.

Signal-based targeting has a failure mode nobody selling it mentions: it doesn't work in small markets.

The logic is sound when your market is large. Filter thousands of plausible companies down to the few hundred showing a reason to talk this quarter, and you've traded volume for relevance.

Now run the same logic on a market of 400 companies. Filter for a hiring signal and you have 11. Filter for funding as well and you have 2. You haven't targeted anything. You've discovered that your entire market isn't doing something this month.

If your total addressable market fits in a spreadsheet you can scroll, the game is different:

Coverage beats filtering. You want all of them, and you want to know which is which.

Signals become timing rather than selection. You email everyone eventually. Signals tell you who to email first and what to open with.

Depth beats freshness. In a market of 400, knowing a company properly is achievable and it's the actual advantage. In a market of 400,000 it isn't, which is why volume plays dominate there.

Most outbound advice, including a fair amount of ours, is written for large markets, because that's where the tooling story is cleanest.

Worth knowing which one you're in before you take any of it.
